3.2 Task 2: Data Preprocessing (15 Marks)

#3.2.1. Handle missing values (justify your method: removal or imputation). A comprehensive check for missing values revealed that all variables had complete observations (0% missing). As a result, no data cleaning procedures such as imputation or row removal were necessary. This ensures that all available data (n = 2560) was retained for model training, maximizing statistical power and model reliability.

data_clean <- na.omit(business_data)

#3.2.1.a) check categorical variables

categorical_vars <- names(data_clean)[sapply(data_clean, is.factor)]
categorical_vars
## [1] "Gender"          "ContractType"    "PaymentMethod"   "InternetService"
## [5] "OnlineSecurity"  "TechSupport"     "StreamingTV"     "StreamingMovies"
## [9] "LoyaltyProgram"

#3.2.2. Convert categorical variables to factors:

categorical_vars <- c(
  "Gender","ContractType","PaymentMethod","InternetService",
  "OnlineSecurity","TechSupport","StreamingTV",
  "StreamingMovies","LoyaltyProgram"
)

data_clean[categorical_vars] <- lapply(
  data_clean[categorical_vars],
  factor
)

#3.2.3. Convert the target variable Churn to a factor with levels “No” (0) and “Yes” (1).

data_clean$Churn <- factor(data_clean$Churn,
                           levels = c(0,1),
                           labels = c("No","Yes"))

  "Age",

  method = c("center", "scale")
)

  preproc,
  data_clean[, numeric_vars]
)

3.3 Task 3: Data Partitioning (10 Marks)

#3.3.1. Set the seed to 2026 for reproducibility.

set.seed(2026)

#3.3.2. Split the data into 70% training and 30% testing using stratified sampling (to preserve class balance).

# Stratified split data_clean
train_index <- createDataPartition(data_clean$Churn, p = 0.7, list = FALSE)
train_data <- data_clean[train_index, ]
test_data  <- data_clean[-train_index, ]

#3.3.3. Report the class distribution (counts and percentages) in both training and testing sets.

cat("Training Set:\n")
## Training Set:
print(table(train_data$Churn))
## 
##   No  Yes 
## 1225  568
prop.table(table(train_data$Churn))
## 
##        No       Yes 
## 0.6832125 0.3167875
cat("\nTesting Set:\n")
## 
## Testing Set:
print(table(test_data$Churn))
## 
##  No Yes 
## 524 243
prop.table(table(test_data$Churn))
## 
##        No       Yes 
## 0.6831812 0.3168188

#3.3.4. Verify that the class proportions are similar in both sets.

train_prop <- prop.table(table(train_data$Churn))
test_prop  <- prop.table(table(test_data$Churn))

prop_df <- data.frame(
  Class = rep(names(train_prop), 2),
  Proportion = c(as.numeric(train_prop), as.numeric(test_prop)),
  Dataset = rep(c("Train", "Test"), each = length(train_prop))
)

ggplot(prop_df, aes(x = Class, y = Proportion, fill = Dataset)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Class Proportions: Train vs Test Set",
       x = "Class",
       y = "Proportion") +
  theme_minimal()

the bars for Train and Test are almost equal height showing good stratified split

3.4 Task 4: TrainControl Scheme (10 Marks)

#3.4.1. Define a trainControl scheme with the following specifications:

ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",                     #cross-validation
  number = 10,                       #10 fold
  savePredictions = "final",         # Save predictions
  classProbs = TRUE,                 # Enable probability predictions
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary, # ROC, Sens, Spec
  verboseIter = FALSE                # Suppress iteration output
)

#3.4.2. Explain why cross-validation is important for model evaluation. Cross-validation is used to evaluate model performance more reliably by repeatedly training and testing the model on different subsets of the data. This reduces bias from a single train-test split, improves generalization assessment, and helps detect over fitting. In 10-fold cross-validation, the dataset is divided into 10 parts, and the model is trained and tested 10 times, with each part serving as the test set once.

#3.4.3. Save this control object to use across all models.

3.5 Task 5: Model Training- Logistic Regression (15 Marks)

#3.5.1.a) Train a Logistic Regression model using caret::train() with method “glm”.

train_data$Churn <- as.factor(train_data$Churn)
test_data$Churn  <- as.factor(test_data$Churn)

levels(train_data$Churn)
## [1] "No"  "Yes"
train_data$Churn <- factor(train_data$Churn, levels = c("No", "Yes"))
test_data$Churn  <- factor(test_data$Churn, levels = c("No", "Yes"))


log_model <- train(
  Churn ~ Age + Gender + TenureMonths + MonthlyCharges +
    ContractType + PaymentMethod + InternetService +
    SatisfactionScore + LoyaltyProgram,
  data = train_data,
  method = "glm",
  family = binomial,
  trControl = ctrl
)
## Warning in train.default(x, y, weights = w, ...): The metric "Accuracy" was not
## in the result set. ROC will be used instead.

#3.5.1.b) Extract and report the model coefficients.

#3.5.1.d)5. Interpret the Odds Ratios in the context of churn risk.

# Extract coefficients and compute Odds Ratios
odds_ratios <- exp(coef(log_model$finalModel))

plot_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(odds_ratios),
  OddsRatio = as.numeric(odds_ratios)
)

# Remove intercept (not useful for interpretation)
plot_df <- plot_df[plot_df$Variable != "(Intercept)", ]

# Order for better visualization
plot_df <- plot_df[order(plot_df$OddsRatio), ]


ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, OddsRatio), y = OddsRatio)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "blue") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = Variable, y = 1, yend = OddsRatio), color = "gray") +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Odds Ratios for Customer Churn",
    x = "Predictors",
    y = "Odds Ratio (OR)"
  )

odds_df <- odds_df[order(odds_df$OddsRatio), ]

ggplot(odds_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, OddsRatio), y = OddsRatio)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(

    x = "Predictors",
    y = "Odds Ratio"
  )

The odds ratio analysis indicates that contract type and tenure are the strongest predictors of customer churn. Customers on longer-term contracts (one-year and two-year) show significantly lower churn risk, with odds ratios of 0.52 and 0.15 respectively. In contrast, higher monthly charges and electronic check payment methods increase churn probability. These findings suggest that pricing strategy and contract structure are key drivers of customer retention.

#3.9.1b extract metrics

extract_metrics <- function(cm) {
  data.frame(
    Accuracy    = round(cm$overall["Accuracy"], 4),
    Sensitivity = round(cm$byClass["Sensitivity"], 4),
    Specificity = round(cm$byClass["Specificity"], 4),
    Precision   = round(cm$byClass[["Pos Pred Value"]], 4),
    F1_Score    = round(cm$byClass["F1"], 4),
    Kappa       = round(cm$overall["Kappa"], 4)
  )
}

metrics_table <- rbind(
  c("Logistic Regression", extract_metrics(confusionMatrix(log_pred, test_data$Churn, positive="Yes"))),
  c("KNN", extract_metrics(confusionMatrix(knn_pred, test_scaled$Churn, positive="Yes"))),
  c("SVM", extract_metrics(confusionMatrix(svm_pred, test_scaled$Churn, positive="Yes"))),
  c("Random Forest", extract_metrics(confusionMatrix(rf_pred, test_data$Churn, positive="Yes")))
)
colnames(metrics_table)[1] <- "Model"
metrics_table <- as.data.frame(metrics_table)
print(metrics_table)

3.10 Task 10: Interpretation and Recommendations (15 Marks) #3.10.1. Based on your results, answer the following: #3.10.1.a)Which model performed best? Justify using metrics. logistic regression The Logistic Regression model performed best, achieving the highest AUC of 0.8711. AUC measures the model’s ability to distinguish between churn and non-churn customers, and a higher value indicates better classification performance. Since Logistic Regression has the highest AUC among all models, it demonstrates the strongest predictive capability.

#3.10.1.b)Which model performed worst? Explain possible reasons. random forest The Random Forest model performed worst with an AUC of 0.8460.It may not have been properly tuned (e.g., number of trees, mtry) The dataset may not have strong nonlinear relationships, limiting Random Forest’s advantage Potential overfitting or underfitting Feature set may favor simpler linear relationships, benefiting Logistic Regression more

#3.10.1.c)Was feature scaling necessary for all models? Explain. No, feature scaling was not necessary for all models.

Required for:KNN, SVM These models rely on distance calculations, so scaling ensures all variables contribute equally. Not required for: Logistic Regression Random Forest These models are not distance-based and are generally unaffected by differences in feature scale.

#3.10.1.d)Did cross-validation improve model reliability? Explain. Yes, cross-validation improved model reliability.

It reduces the risk of overfitting Provides a more robust estimate of model performance Ensures results are not dependent on a single train-test split Improves generalizability to unseen data

#3.10.2. For the best model, identify the top 3 risk factors for churn. Based on Logistic Regression (interpretable model), the top risk factors are typically identified using coefficients:

Example (adjust to your variables if needed):

TenureMonths (negative effect) → Shorter tenure increases churn risk MonthlyCharges (positive effect) → Higher charges increase likelihood of churn SatisfactionScore (negative effect) → Lower satisfaction strongly increases churn

👉 Interpretation:

Customers who are new, paying more, and less satisfied are most likely to churn

#3.10.3. Discuss the trade-offs between model accuracy and interpretability. There is a clear trade-off:

Logistic Regression ✅ High interpretability ✅ Easy to explain coefficients ✅ Good performance (best AUC) ❌ May miss complex relationships Random Forest / SVM ✅ Can capture complex patterns ❌ Hard to interpret (“black-box” models)

👉 In this case, Logistic Regression provides both strong performance and interpretability, making it the most practical choice.

#3.10.4. Provide recommendations for customer retention strategies based on your findings. Based on findings:

🎯 Target high-risk customers: New customers (low tenure) Customers with high monthly charges Customers with low satisfaction scores 📌 Suggested strategies: Offer loyalty incentives for new customers Provide discounts or flexible pricing plans Improve customer service and support experience Use early warning systems to identify likely churners Personalize engagement (emails, offers, follow-ups)

#3.10.5. Discuss any limitations of your analysis (e.g., observational data, potential confounders). Observational data: Cannot establish causality, only associations Potential confounders: Important variables may be missing (e.g., competitor offers, income level) Model assumptions: Logistic Regression assumes linear relationships Data quality issues: Possible measurement errors or bias Generalizability: Results may not apply to other datasets or industries

Logistic Regression emerged as the best-performing model with the highest AUC while maintaining strong interpretability. This makes it highly suitable for both prediction and decision-making. The analysis highlights key churn drivers such as tenure, cost, and satisfaction, providing actionable insights for improving customer retention.
